## The data, and why the unit of observation matters

- 8 source tables joined: 91,300 sales records, 50 menu items, 8 categories, R07 in Minneapolis, 2021–2025 (1,826 days)
- One sales row = one menu item on one date, not a customer — two outcomes kept separate: quantity per item-day vs total units per restaurant-day
- Data quality found, not hidden: 365 missing quantities, 14 temperatures coded -99, 55 dates with no weather record

::: {.notes}
Most early mistakes in this class came from not knowing what a row was. I fixed that first, before any chart or model.
:::

## What sells: drinks carry the volume

- Drinks lead unit demand; a small group of familiar items carries much of the volume
- Burgers lead estimated total food-cost margin — volume and value point to different decisions
- Category totals and typical item-day quantities answer different questions, and both are needed

::: {.notes}
Volume tells the owner what must never run out. Margin tells the owner what is worth promoting. Stage 1 kept those two stories separate.
:::

## When it sells: demand has a calendar rhythm

- Demand rises into summer and varies by weekday; categories do not share one seasonal shape
- Averages alone mislead — weekday distributions show the spread within each day, not just the center
- This rhythm is exactly what the Stage 2 models are asked to learn

::: {.notes}
The calendar pattern in this slide is the hypothesis Stage 2 tests: if demand has a rhythm, a model using calendar predictors should beat a simple average.
:::

## Relationships worth testing, and one that failed

- Promotions, weather, and events show associations worth modeling
- Price and preparation time show no clear overall linear pattern with item-day quantity
- The negative result is kept on purpose: a weak scatterplot is a finding, not a failure to hide

::: {.notes}
Stage 1 ended with hypotheses, not conclusions. That set up the modeling honestly — I only modeled predictors that had a reason to be there.
:::

## Week 6: the project is a Quarto website

- Every page renders from the same data and code, with "Show R code" on every chart
- No hand-typed numbers anywhere on the site — every number is computed from the data
- If a number cannot be recomputed, it does not go on the site

::: {.notes}
Reproducibility was the Week 6 lesson. It also made Stage 2 easier: the modeling page reuses the same daily-demand table the report already built.
:::

## Week 8: my first model, and the split-first rule

- Target: total daily demand (units per restaurant-day), one row per date — a regression problem
- 80/20 split with seed 681, before any preprocessing: 1,460 training days, 366 test days
- Recipe v1 (lean): calendar + headline weather, median imputation for numbers, dummies for categories, no normalization for a plain linear model

::: {.notes}
The biggest Week 8 lesson: the recipe is prepped inside the workflow on training data only. Prep on the full data and the test set leaks into the model.
:::

## Week 9: two recipes, four model specs, five workflows

- Recipe v2 (full) adds season, event group, and precipitation type; mode imputation for text; normalize predictors only, never the outcome
- Specs: linear regression (lm), lasso (glmnet, mixture 1), ridge (glmnet, mixture 0 — Week 12 Activity 3 fits ridge in class), decision tree (rpart), all in regression mode
- Five workflows compared, plus two baselines; random forest and boosting appear in class only in prose, so they are left as a future extension, not presented as class work

::: {.notes}
Week 9 was about each tidymodels package having one job: rsample splits, recipes prep, parsnip specifies, workflows combine. The bugs I learned to avoid: recipe vs baked data, median vs mode imputation, classification mode on a numeric outcome.
:::

## Week 10: predictions, judged against baselines

- Every workflow predicts the same held-out test days; the overall-mean and weekday-average baselines predict them too
- Predicted-vs-actual and residuals-over-time charts show where a model fails, not just how much
- A model that cannot beat the weekday average has learned nothing the calendar did not already say

::: {.notes}
The baselines keep the results honest. In the end every real model beat them by a wide margin, which is what makes the winner's number believable.
:::

## Weeks 11–12: assessment before recommendation

| Model | Test RMSE | Test MAE | Test R2 | CV RMSE | Time-test RMSE | Time-test MAE | Time-test R2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LM + Recipe v2 | 130.7 | 84.8 | 0.908 | 110.6 | 134.2 | 96.8 | 0.924 |
| Lasso + Recipe v2 | 130.8 | 85.0 | 0.908 | 110.8 | 134.1 | 96.9 | 0.924 |
| Ridge + Recipe v2 | 137.8 | 89.8 | 0.901 | 116.1 | 137.8 | 100.8 | 0.919 |
| Tree + Recipe v2 | 192.7 | 140.7 | 0.799 | 183.2 | 178.8 | 131.5 | 0.835 |
| LM + Recipe v1 | 196.3 | 114.0 | 0.790 | 166.4 | 169.6 | 108.6 | 0.856 |
| Baseline: weekday average | 383.0 | 294.1 | 0.201 | — | 373.1 | 289.7 | 0.168 |
| Baseline: overall mean | 428.0 | 317.8 | — | — | 407.4 | 318.2 | — |

- Three views of the same models: random-split test, 5-fold cross-validation, and a time split (train 2021–2024, test 2025)
- Only one thing tuned: the lasso penalty, on the CV folds, never on the test set

::: {.notes}
Weeks 11–12 changed my order of work: metrics first, interpretation second, recommendation last. Note the time split: lasso essentially ties the winner there, 134.1 against 134.2, so I am not claiming a large gap between the top two.
:::

## The winner: a plain linear model with the full recipe

- **LM + Recipe v2** — test RMSE 130.7, test MAE 84.8, test R2 0.908; it also leads on CV (110.6) and holds up on the unseen year (time-test RMSE 134.2, R2 0.924)
- Largest drivers (normalized scale): July +216.3, June +199.1, August +186.6, Saturday +162.9, May +145.6, September +121.9
- Also in the top ten: no special event -121.1, Friday +111.0, Sunday +98.1, October +79.5 — summer, weekends, and event days drive demand
- In business terms: a typical day's prediction is off by about **85 units per day** — a prep buffer and staffing range, not an exact order quantity

::: {.notes}
The winner is not the fanciest model. The full recipe beat the lean one by a wide margin, and then a plain linear model on that recipe was enough. The summer and Saturday effects match what Stage 1 found descriptively, which is a good consistency check.
:::

## What did not work

- Lean Recipe v1 was the worst model (test RMSE 196.3): the added season, event, and precipitation predictors in v2 mattered
- The decision tree was clearly worse (192.7) than every linear-family model on this data
- Two build errors were caught by checking my own output: a results table that did not print, and a winner label that picked the wrong row — both found because the numbers on the page are checked against each other, and both fixed before reporting

::: {.notes}
I include this slide because verification is part of the work. The check that caught the problems was simple: the recommendation on the page has to agree with the ranked table above it. If I had not compared them, I would have presented the wrong winner.
:::

## Limitations

- One restaurant only (R07, Minneapolis); nothing transfers to another location without refitting and re-assessing
- Weather is association, not cause — and at planning time only forecast weather is available, which is less accurate than the recorded weather used here
- Monthly marketing was excluded from the daily models on purpose: repeating monthly spend on daily rows would invent daily precision the data does not have

::: {.notes}
Every limit here is a data limit, not a model limit. Better inputs — item-level promotions, real weather forecasts — would beat a fancier model. The random split is also optimistic next to the time split, which is why both are reported.
:::

## What I learned, in one slide

- First analysis (Stage 1): describe honestly, keep the unit of observation straight, report negative results
- Updated analysis (Stage 2): split first, compare against baselines, assess three ways before recommending anything
- Next step if I continued: item-level promotion data and real weather forecasts as predictors

::: {.notes}
The course moved me from "what happened" to "what can we predict, and how wrong might we be" — and to saying the second part out loud.
:::
